newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries bears throw in towel at 6.50 pct.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries bears throw in towel at 6.50 pct.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended sharply higher on Wednesday, pulled up by the long end where the 30-year bond yield broke the 6.50-percent psychological barrier to force the last bears back into the market.
The rally was kicked off by good inflation news as the Consumer Price Index rose a mere 0.1 percent in June.

"In the past, we had rallies triggered by weak data. Now, we don't have weak economic data, we have good inflation news that continue to surprise us," said senior economist John Ryding at Bear, Stearns and Co.
For the past 12 months through June, the CPI has been rising at only 2.3 percent.
U.S. consumer inflation may be trending still lower since the CPI inched up by just 0.1 percent in five of the first six months of this year, or at an annualized rate of 1.5 percent.
"This is changing the thinking of many people. You can have 3.0-percent growth and low unemployment, and inflation can still go down," Ryding emphasized.
In late trading, the 30-year bond was up 30/32 at a session high of 101-31/32 to yield 6.47 percent -- its lowest since December 1996.
Analysts noted the bond yield last traded below 6.50 percent at the time Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned about "irrational exhuberance" in financial markets.

The declining market rates environment helped the Dow Jones industrial average rocket to a close above the 8000 barrier for the first time. The Dow traded about 1650 points lower when Greenspan made the "exhuberance" comments.

"It's a brave new world. The market is now going to focus on what Greenspan will say next week because he believes you can have good economic performance without inflation, but he also believes in the Phillips Curve," Ryding added.

The Phillips Curve theory links low unemployment with inflationary pressures. According to models built on that theory, U.S. inflation should be rising -- not declining -- with an unemployment rate below 5.0 percent.
Greenspan will present his views on growth and monetary policy in a mandatory testimony before Congress next week.
Ryding said good growth and low inflation were making it possible to simultaneously fuel rallies in stocks and bonds.
"The mortgage guys will kick in now. There are about $140 billion of mortgages refinanceable at these rates," added Ryding who forecast a 6-1/4-percent long bond yield soon.
Mortgage holders tend to shift funds to Treasuries when faced with heavy refinancing and pre-payments.
Economist Alan Levenson at Aubrey G. Lanston said the market action reflected "the pain of being short."

"It was not any particular news since we knew inflation is low. People who tried to short the market got frustrated," Levenson said. "The market did better and the curve flattened because of duration expensions play."
The front end of the U.S. curve offers no reward with the one-year bill yielding no more than the 5.50-percent overnight federal funds rate.

Levenson said U.S. markets were not "irrationally exuberant, given the economic scenario and the Fed legitimally out of the picture," although he cautioned that when "you shake out the residual bears out of the market, that's when the market may decide to turn around."
The two-year note was up 3/32 at 100-8/32 to yield 5.86 percent, the five-year up 9/32 at 100-21/32 and 6.09 percent, and the 10-year note up 15/32 at 103-15/32 and 6.19 percent.
The three-month bill was down one point at a discount rate of 5.05 percent, the six-month down two at 5.09 percent and the one-year bills down three at 5.21 percent.
